result: ICV (a measure of sustained attention) significantly decreased from ages 14 to 23, indicating improvement in sustained attention over adolescence. Individual differences in ICV were significantly correlated across all three timepoints (ages 14, 19, and 23).
evaluation: Claims C24-C26 and C72 provide converging evidence from linear mixed model analysis showing significant age-related decreases in ICV with appropriate statistical tests (all p<0.001) and significant correlations between timepoints (p<2.8e-7). The findings are consistent with prior literature (C72) and demonstrate both developmental change and individual stability.

result: Brain networks derived from Go trials significantly predicted ICV at all three ages (14, 19, and 23), with positive, negative, and combined networks showing significant correlations (r=0.25-0.38, all p<0.001). Network strength was significantly correlated across timepoints.
evaluation: Claims C27-C30 demonstrate robust predictive performance using CPM analysis with appropriate cross-validation. The correlations are statistically significant and show consistent patterns across ages. Network strength correlations across timepoints (C30) support the stability of individual differences.

result: Brain networks derived from Successful stop trials significantly predicted ICV at all three ages, though with somewhat lower correlations (r=0.12-0.24) than Go trial networks. Network strength was significantly correlated across timepoints.
evaluation: Claims C31-C34 show significant predictive performance for Successful stop trial networks, though effect sizes are smaller than Go trial networks. All correlations are statistically significant with appropriate corrections. The consistency across timepoints supports the robustness of these networks.

result: The sustained attention networks showed specificity to sustained attention, being robustly correlated with RVP task performance rather than other cognitive measures.
evaluation: Claims C35 and C71 demonstrate specificity through correlations with the RVP task (a validated sustained attention measure) at ages 14 and 19 (all p<0.028), with weaker or absent correlations with other cognitive measures. This supports the construct validity of the identified networks.

result: Sustained attention networks defined at earlier timepoints successfully predicted ICV at later timepoints, with networks from Go trials showing stronger temporal generalization (r=0.12-0.31) than Successful stop trials (r=0.11-0.17). This demonstrates that individual differences in sustained attention networks are preserved throughout development.
evaluation: Claims C36-C41 and C73 provide strong evidence for temporal stability of predictive networks with all correlations significant at p<0.001. The cross-timepoint predictions demonstrate that networks identified at one age can predict behavior years later, supporting the inference in C73 about preserved individual differences.

result: Sustained attention networks generalized to an external dataset (STRATIFY), with networks from both Go trials (r=0.34-0.35) and Successful stop trials (r=0.22-0.26) significantly predicting ICV in independent participants aged 23.
evaluation: Claims C42-C43 demonstrate successful external validation with statistically significant predictions (all p<0.001) in an independent dataset. This provides strong evidence for the generalizability and robustness of the identified networks beyond the training sample.

result: Exploratory factor analysis of substance use data identified two factors at age 14 (alcohol; cigarette and cannabis use) and three factors at ages 19 and 23 (alcohol; cigarette and cannabis use; other drug use).
evaluation: Claims C44-C45 describe appropriate data reduction using exploratory factor analysis with adequate sample adequacy (KMO 0.66-0.81) and significant Bartlett's tests. The factor structure is consistent with known patterns of substance co-use.

result: ICV was significantly correlated with cigarette and cannabis use (Cig+CB) both within timepoints (ages 19 and 23) and across timepoints, with correlations ranging from Rho=0.13-0.17 after FDR correction.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 show consistent correlations between ICV and Cig+CB with appropriate statistical corrections (FDR q<0.05). The effect sizes are modest but consistent, supporting an association between poorer sustained attention and substance use.

result: Brain network strength from both Go trials and Successful stop trials was significantly correlated with Cig+CB, both within and across timepoints, after FDR correction.
evaluation: Claims C51-C55 demonstrate significant correlations between brain network activity and substance use with appropriate multiple comparison corrections. The correlations are modest (Rho=0.08-0.16) but consistent across different network types and timepoints.

result: Higher ICV (poorer sustained attention) and associated brain network patterns at age 14 predicted greater increases in cigarette and cannabis use from ages 14 to 23, but substance use did not predict changes in ICV or brain activity. This establishes a directional relationship where poor sustained attention precedes increased substance use.
evaluation: Claims C56-C59 from the bivariate latent change score model provide strong evidence for directionality. The significant lagged effects of ICV/brain activity on Cig+CB changes (Std. β=0.09-0.12, p<0.006) with no reverse effects (C56) support the main conclusion (C2, C76) that poor sustained attention predicts subsequent substance use rather than vice versa.

result: No significant bidirectional relationships were found between alcohol use and ICV/brain activity after FDR correction.
evaluation: Claim C60 reports null findings with appropriate statistical corrections (all p>0.011 after FDR). This demonstrates specificity of the sustained attention-substance use relationship to cigarette and cannabis use rather than all substances.

result: Working memory performance at baseline did not show significant differences in cigarette and cannabis use, demonstrating specificity of sustained attention in predicting substance use.
evaluation: Claim C87 provides important negative control evidence showing that the relationship between cognitive function and substance use is specific to sustained attention rather than general cognitive ability. This strengthens the specificity of the main findings.

result: Brain networks of sustained attention are robust, consistent across development, and able to predict aspects of later substance use.
evaluation: Claims C3 and C5 represent the main conclusions synthesizing multiple findings. These are well-supported by the convergent evidence from temporal stability (C36-C41), external validation (C42-C43), and longitudinal prediction of substance use (C57-C59).

result: The manuscript provides extensive background on sustained attention, its development, neuroanatomy, relationship to substance use, and underlying neurobiology based on prior literature.
evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C23, C61-C70, C74-C75, C86, and C88 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These provide the scientific context and rationale for the current study. The citations appear appropriate and accurately represent the cited work.

result: The manuscript describes the methodological approach including the ICV measure, datasets (IMAGEN and STRATIFY), stop signal task, CPM analysis, and latent change score modeling.
evaluation: Claims C77-C85 describe the methods with appropriate detail and citations. The ICV measure is well-defined (C77-C79), datasets are adequately described (C80-C81), and analytical approaches are justified with citations (C83-C85). These methodological choices are appropriate for the research questions.
